name: AI/ML track
duration: About 12 months at 10 hours a week
blurb: Python, the maths you actually need, classic machine learning, testing models honestly, deep learning, transformers, vision, generative models, reinforcement learning and shipping models. The foundation every AI job assumes.
start_if: Start here if you're new to coding or AI, or you want ML engineer, data scientist or research roles.

roles.title: Machine learning engineer
roles.text: Builds, ships and looks after models inside real products. The most common AI job. Every stage matters, stages 3, 4 and 10 most.

roles.title: Data scientist
roles.text: Finds answers in data and builds models that support decisions. Stages 1 to 4 and 11 matter most.

roles.title: AI engineer
roles.text: Builds apps on top of existing models. Do stages 1 to 6 here, then move to the Gen AI track.

roles.title: Research engineer
roles.text: Trains and studies new models. Needs strong maths (stage 2) and stages 5 to 9 in depth; often a master's or PhD later.

phases.title: Foundations
phases.text: Python, data tools and just enough maths to understand what a model does.

phases.title: Core machine learning
phases.text: The classic models that still run most businesses, and how to test any model honestly.

phases.title: Deep learning
phases.text: Neural networks from scratch, then the transformers behind LLMs and the models that see.

phases.title: Beyond prediction
phases.text: Models that create images and agents that learn by trial and error.

phases.title: Ship it and get hired
phases.text: Put models in front of people safely and fairly, then turn your work into proof.

overview.pace_note: Timings assume about 10 hours a week. Studying full time? Roughly halve them. Already code in Python? Skim stage 1.

checks.title: Beat a baseline
checks.text: Start every project with the simplest possible model. If your fancy model can't beat it, something is wrong.

checks.title: Explain it without notes
checks.text: After each stage, explain its main idea out loud in two minutes. The gaps show up fast.

checks.title: Rebuild without the tutorial
checks.text: Rebuild one thing from each stage without looking. Copying along doesn't count.

checks.title: Show your work
checks.text: Push every project to GitHub, share it on Kaggle and ask for feedback. Other eyes catch what you miss.

stages.title: Python, data and the everyday tools
stages.why: Every model, notebook and API you'll touch is Python, and most real data sits in SQL databases. Get comfortable with both before anything else.
topics: SQL: select, filter, join, group by
Jupyter, Google Colab and VS Code

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python
resources.note: The clearest start if you've never coded.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Python
resources.note: Short lessons with exercises in the browser.

resources.title: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners
Kaggle Learn: Intro to SQL
resources.note: Real queries on real datasets, in the browser.

resources.title: SQLBolt
resources.note: Interactive SQL lessons, one idea at a time.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
resources.note: The terminal, Git and tools nobody teaches in class.

resources.title: GitHub Skills
resources.note: Learn Git by doing it in a real repo.

project.title: Explore a real dataset
project.text: Pick a dataset you care about (IPL matches, your city's weather, exam results from Kaggle). Load it into SQLite and answer 5 questions with SQL, then clean it with Pandas, make 5 charts, write what you found, and push the notebook to GitHub.
project.check: Someone else can clone your repo, run the notebook top to bottom without errors, and read your 5 findings in the README.

done_when: You can write functions and a small class without looking things up
You can load, clean and group a CSV in Pandas, and write the same query in SQL
Your notebook is on GitHub with a readable README
mistakes: Writing Python loops over rows when one NumPy or Pandas operation would do it
Keeping everything in one giant notebook with cells that only work in a certain order
Not using Git until the end, then losing work

stages.title: The maths you actually need
stages.why: Not a maths degree: just enough linear algebra, calculus and probability to understand what a model is doing and to fix it when it breaks.
topics: Eigenvectors and SVD (the idea behind PCA and LoRA)
Derivatives, gradients and the chain rule
Gradient descent and the learning rate
Maximum likelihood: why training means minimising a loss
Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence (the intuition)

resources.title: Essence of Linear Algebra
resources.note: Watch this first: pictures before formulas.

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning and Data Science
resources.note: Maths taught with Python, aimed at ML beginners.

resources.title: Seeing Theory
resources.note: Probability and statistics you can play with.

resources.title: StatQuest
resources.note: Short, friendly explanations of every stats and ML idea.

resources.title: Linear Algebra (18.06)
resources.note: Go deeper once the 3Blue1Brown pictures click.

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
resources.note: Free PDF. Use as a reference, not cover to cover.

project.title: Gradient descent by hand
project.text: Implement linear regression with gradient descent in plain NumPy, no ML libraries. Plot the loss going down, try a learning rate that's too big and explain what happens, then check your answer against the closed-form solution.
project.check: Your gradient descent weights match NumPy's least-squares answer to 3 decimal places.

done_when: You can explain a dot product and a gradient in your own words
You can say why we take small steps downhill to train a model
You can explain why classification models minimise cross-entropy
You know what mean, variance and a normal distribution are
mistakes: Trying to finish a whole maths textbook before writing any ML code
Memorising formulas without being able to draw what they mean
Skipping matrix shapes, then fighting shape errors in every model

stages.title: Classic machine learning
stages.why: Most real business problems on tables of data (fraud, credit, sales, ranking) are still solved with these models. They're fast, cheap and easy to explain, and on tabular data they often beat deep learning.
topics: Feature engineering: scaling, one-hot and target encoding

resources.title: Machine Learning Specialization
resources.note: The classic start. Audit for free, or apply for Coursera financial aid for the certificate.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to Machine Learning
resources.note: Then take Intermediate Machine Learning.

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning (with Python)
resources.note: Free PDF. The friendliest serious ML textbook.

resources.title: XGBoost documentation
resources.note: Start with the Python tutorials.

resources.title: Hands-On Machine Learning (3rd edition) notebooks
resources.note: The notebooks are free; the book itself is paid and worth it.

resources.title: CS229: Machine Learning
resources.note: Advanced: the maths behind every model. Come back to it later.

project.title: Two Kaggle problems, done properly
project.text: Solve Kaggle's Titanic (classification) and House Prices (regression) with scikit-learn pipelines. Compare a simple model, a random forest and XGBoost with cross-validation, and write down which features mattered and why.
project.check: Your best model beats a simple baseline in cross-validation, and your Kaggle leaderboard score is close to your own validation score.

done_when: You never judge a model on the data it trained on
You can explain what regularisation does and when you need it
You can explain why gradient boosting beat (or lost to) logistic regression on your data
mistakes: Filling missing values or scaling on the whole dataset before splitting (that's leakage)
Reaching for deep learning on table data where gradient boosting wins
Trusting one lucky train/test split instead of cross-validation

stages.title: Test models honestly
stages.why: A model that looks 99% accurate can be useless. Learn to measure properly before you trust any number, yours or anyone else's. This is what separates engineers from tutorial-followers.
topics: Time-series splits: never train on the future
Group splits: the same person never in both sets
Data leakage and how to catch it
Confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1
ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC for rare events
Bias vs variance, underfitting vs overfitting

resources.title: Classification: accuracy, precision and recall
resources.note: The clearest explanation of why accuracy misleads.

resources.title: Common pitfalls and recommended practices
resources.note: Short, and it covers leakage properly.

resources.title: Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance
resources.note: Stratified, group and time-series splits with code.

resources.title: Data Leakage
resources.note: Part of Intermediate Machine Learning.

resources.title: Machine Learning Fundamentals: Bias and Variance
Optuna
resources.note: Tunes hyperparameters for you, far better than grid search.

project.title: Break your own model
project.text: Use Kaggle's Credit Card Fraud dataset (0.17% fraud). Show that “always say not fraud” scores 99.8% accuracy. Build a real model and report precision, recall and PR-AUC instead. Then add a leak on purpose (a feature computed from the whole dataset) and show how it inflates the score.
project.check: Your write-up shows the baseline, the leaky score and the honest score side by side, and your honest PR-AUC clearly beats the baseline.

done_when: You always compare against a baseline
You can choose between precision and recall for a real problem and justify it
You can explain data leakage with an example
You can read a learning curve and say whether a model underfits or overfits
mistakes: Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data
Shuffling time-series data, so the model peeks at the future
Checking the test set again and again until the number looks good

stages.title: Deep learning
stages.why: Neural networks power everything in the rest of this track and the Gen AI track. Build one from scratch once, and nothing after feels like magic.
topics: Learning-rate schedules, warmup and gradient clipping
Overfitting fixes: augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping

resources.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
resources.note: Builds a neural network engine from scratch. The single best resource here.

resources.title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders
resources.note: Top-down and practical: working models from lesson one.

resources.title: Dive into Deep Learning
resources.note: Free interactive book with runnable code.

resources.title: Understanding Deep Learning
resources.note: Free PDF with excellent diagrams and notebooks.

resources.title: Deep Learning
resources.note: The classic reference. Read chapters when you need them.

project.title: From micrograd to a real classifier
project.text: Follow Karpathy's micrograd lecture and build it yourself. Then train a CNN in PyTorch on a small image dataset you collect (for example, Indian dishes), first from scratch and then with transfer learning from a pretrained ResNet.
project.check: Transfer learning beats your from-scratch model on the same validation set, and you can show the loss curves for both.

done_when: You can write a PyTorch training loop without copying it
You can explain backpropagation with a small example
You know how to spot and fix overfitting
You can say why skip connections let very deep networks train
mistakes: Forgetting model.eval() and torch.no_grad() when evaluating
A learning rate so high the loss turns into NaN
Not normalising inputs
Training for hours without checking the GPU is actually being used

stages.title: Language models and transformers
stages.why: Every LLM is a transformer trained to predict the next token. Build a small one yourself and the Gen AI track will make complete sense.
topics: RNNs and LSTMs, and why they were slow
The Transformer: multi-head attention, positions, layer norm

resources.title: The Illustrated Transformer
resources.note: Read this before any code: the whole idea in pictures.

resources.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out
resources.note: Two hours that demystify every LLM.

resources.title: Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch): code
resources.note: The code and videos are free; the book is paid.

resources.title: CS224n: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
LLM Course
resources.note: Transformers, tokenizers and fine-tuning, hands-on.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need
resources.note: The paper that started it. Read it after the pictures and the code.

resources.title: Speech and Language Processing
resources.note: Free draft. The reference for NLP.

project.title: Your own tiny GPT, then a real fine-tune
project.text: Train a small GPT from scratch on a text you like (Premchand stories, film dialogues, your college's notices). Then fine-tune DistilBERT for sentiment on Indian product reviews and compare it with a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline.
project.check: Validation loss goes down steadily, generated samples look like the training text, and fine-tuned DistilBERT beats the baseline's F1.

done_when: You can explain self-attention with a small example
You can say why transformers train faster than RNNs
You have trained a small language model from scratch
You can explain when to use BERT-style vs GPT-style models
mistakes: Forgetting the causal mask, so the model cheats by seeing future tokens
Comparing models with different tokenizers by raw loss
Fine-tuning a big model before trying a simple baseline

stages.title: Computer vision beyond classification
stages.why: Real vision products don't just label a photo: they find things, outline them and run fast on small devices. Learn detection, segmentation and how to make models quick.
topics: Exporting to ONNX for fast inference

resources.title: CS231n: Deep Learning for Computer Vision
resources.note: Lectures and notes are free online.

resources.title: Ultralytics YOLO docs
resources.note: Train a detector on your own data in an afternoon.

resources.title: Roboflow Universe
resources.note: Thousands of labelled datasets, and a tool to label your own.

resources.title: ONNX Runtime
resources.note: Run models fast on CPUs and phones.

project.title: Detect something useful
project.text: Collect and label about 200 images of something that matters where you live (potholes, helmets on two-wheelers, crop diseases). Fine-tune a YOLO model, export it to ONNX, and run it on a phone video.
project.check: You report mAP@50 on images the model never saw, and it runs in real time on a laptop CPU.

done_when: You can explain IoU and mAP
You have trained a detector on data you labelled
You can make a model faster with export and quantisation
mistakes: Frames from the same video in both training and test sets (leakage again)
Measuring detection with accuracy instead of mAP
Too few examples of the rare classes you care about most

stages.title: Generative models: GANs, VAEs and diffusion
stages.why: Models that create images, audio and video are built on a few ideas. Learn them, and tools like Stable Diffusion stop being black boxes.
topics: Text-to-image: how text guides an image

resources.title: What are Diffusion Models?
resources.note: Deep but clear. Read after the course.

project.title: Generate, then judge
project.text: Train a small GAN or VAE on Fashion-MNIST and save samples as training goes. Then use Diffusers to generate images with a pretrained diffusion model and compare the two approaches.
project.check: You can show samples improving over training and explain one failure you saw, such as mode collapse.

done_when: You can explain how a GAN trains
You can explain the noise-in, noise-out idea behind diffusion
You can say why generated faces need consent
mistakes: Judging a generator only by a few good-looking samples
Letting the discriminator get far stronger than the generator
Using real people's photos without consent

stages.title: Reinforcement learning
stages.why: Some problems have no labels, only rewards: games, robots, recommendations and training LLMs to follow instructions (RLHF). Reinforcement learning is how models learn from trial and error.
topics: Deep Q-Networks: replay buffers and target networks
RL for language models: RLHF and GRPO

resources.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning Course
resources.note: Hands-on from Q-learning to PPO.

resources.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction
resources.note: Free PDF. The classic.

resources.title: Gymnasium
resources.note: The standard set of practice environments.

resources.title: Illustrating Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
resources.note: How RL turns a base model into an assistant.

project.title: Teach an agent to balance, then land
project.text: Solve CartPole with a Deep Q-Network you write yourself, then train PPO with Stable-Baselines3 on LunarLander. Plot the average reward as training goes.
project.check: The average reward over 100 episodes passes the environment's “solved” mark: 475 for CartPole, 200 for LunarLander.

done_when: You can explain states, actions, rewards and discounting
You can say why DQN needs a replay buffer
You can explain what RLHF adds to a language model
mistakes: Judging an agent by one lucky episode
A reward the agent can game without solving the task
Comparing runs without fixing the random seed

stages.title: Ship it: MLOps and deployment
stages.why: A model in a notebook helps nobody. Learn to serve it, version it, test it automatically and notice when it quietly gets worse once real people use it.
topics: APIs with FastAPI and input validation
Demos with Gradio on Hugging Face Spaces
Automated tests and deploys with GitHub Actions
Cloud basics: SageMaker, Vertex AI or Azure ML, and GPU costs

resources.title: Made With ML
resources.note: Production ML end to end, written for engineers.

resources.title: MLOps Zoomcamp
resources.note: Free cohort course with homework and a community.

resources.title: MLflow
resources.note: Track every experiment and which model is live.

resources.title: DVC: Get Started
resources.note: Version datasets without putting them in Git.

resources.title: Evidently
resources.note: Drift and data-quality reports in a few lines.

resources.title: Hugging Face Spaces
resources.note: Free hosting for demos.

resources.title: Modal
resources.note: Run heavy models on cloud GPUs by the second.

project.title: Put your model on the internet, properly
project.text: Take your stage 4 or 7 model. Wrap it in a FastAPI service inside Docker, track training runs with MLflow, version the data with DVC, run tests on every push with GitHub Actions, add a Gradio demo on Hugging Face Spaces, and log every prediction.
project.check: Anyone can try it from a link, a push runs your tests automatically, and when you feed it shifted data on purpose, your Evidently drift report flags it.

done_when: Anyone can try your model from a link
Your service runs the same on your laptop and in the cloud
You can say which data and code trained the model that's live
You can tell when it starts getting worse
mistakes: Preparing inputs one way in training and another way in the API
No input validation, so one bad request crashes the service
Never looking at the model again after launch

stages.title: Responsible AI: fairness, privacy and explanations
stages.why: Models make decisions about people: loans, jobs, admissions. Knowing how they fail some groups, how to explain them and what the law says about personal data is part of the job, not an extra.
topics: Where bias comes from: data, labels and proxies
Fairness metrics: demographic parity, equal opportunity
India's DPDP Act 2023 and Europe's GDPR
UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to AI Ethics
resources.note: Short and practical.

resources.title: Fairlearn
resources.note: Measure and reduce unfairness in scikit-learn models.

resources.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

project.title: Audit a model
project.text: Take a model you built (or train one on the UCI Adult income dataset). Measure its results for each group, explain its predictions with SHAP, and write a model card that says what it's for, how it was tested and where it fails.
project.check: Your model card shows results per group, names at least one real limitation and says who should not use the model.

done_when: You can name three ways bias gets into a model
You can measure a model's results per group
You can explain one prediction with SHAP
You know the basics of India's data protection law
mistakes: Deleting the sensitive column and assuming the model is now fair (other columns act as proxies)
Reporting one overall score that hides a group the model fails
Collecting personal data without clear consent

stages.title: Portfolio, interviews and staying current
stages.why: Turn what you built into proof. Recruiters look for finished projects you can explain, not certificates. And AI moves fast, so build a habit of keeping up.
topics: ML interview questions: bias-variance, gradient descent, metrics
Coding interviews: data structures and algorithms

resources.title: Designing Machine Learning Systems
resources.note: The best book on ML system design interviews.

resources.title: NeetCode
resources.note: Structured practice for coding interviews.

resources.title: The Batch
resources.note: A weekly newsletter on what matters in AI.

resources.title: Daily Papers
resources.note: The easiest way to follow new research.

project.title: Four projects that prove it
project.text: Polish four projects from this track: a tabular model tested honestly (stages 3–4), a vision system (stage 7), a transformer from scratch (stage 6) and a deployed, monitored service (stage 10). Each gets a clear README, a live demo, what didn't work and what you'd do next. Then enter one Kaggle competition.
project.check: A stranger can open each repo, understand it from the README and try the live demo within 10 minutes.

done_when: Four projects with live demos and honest READMEs
You can walk an interviewer through one project's trade-offs in five minutes
You read one paper or newsletter a week
mistakes: Listing certificates instead of projects
Projects copied from tutorials with nothing of your own
Not being able to explain your own code in an interview

name: Gen AI track
duration: About 4 months at 8–10 hours a week
blurb: How LLMs really work, then using them well: APIs, RAG, agents, evals, fine-tuning and shipping real AI products.
start_if: Start here if you know basic Python. Do AI/ML stages 1 to 4 first if you want to understand what's underneath.

stages.title: How LLMs actually work
stages.why: Before building with LLMs, know what they are: next-word predictors trained on huge amounts of text. It explains both their magic and their mistakes.

resources.title: Intro to Large Language Models
resources.note: One hour, the best overview there is.

resources.title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
resources.note: Longer and deeper: pre-training to reasoning models.

resources.title: Neural Networks (Transformer chapters)
resources.note: Beautiful visual explanations of attention.

resources.title: Tiktokenizer
resources.note: Type text and see exactly how a model splits it into tokens.

project.title: Explain it to a friend
project.text: Write a one-page explainer (with pictures) of how an LLM turns your question into an answer, token by token. Use Tiktokenizer to show real tokens.

done_when: You can explain tokens, embeddings and attention without jargon
You can say why an LLM confidently makes things up

stages.title: Use LLM APIs well
stages.why: Most Gen AI products are built on APIs. Learn prompting, structured outputs, streaming and costs properly.

resources.title: Google AI Studio
resources.note: A free Gemini API key: the easiest way to start without paying.

resources.title: Pydantic
resources.note: Validate the JSON a model gives you.

resources.title: Vercel AI SDK
resources.note: If you build in TypeScript.

project.title: A study helper that returns clean data
project.text: Build a command-line helper that turns a chapter of your notes into flashcards as validated JSON, streams the answer, retries on errors, and prints what each run cost.

done_when: Your app never crashes on a bad model reply
You get the same JSON shape every time
You know roughly what 1,000 requests would cost

stages.title: Build a small GPT from scratch
stages.why: Code the Transformer yourself once. After this, papers, model cards and fine-tuning all make sense.

resources.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code
Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)
resources.note: The code and videos are free; the book is paid.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need
resources.note: The original Transformer paper. Read it after the videos.

project.title: Your own tiny GPT
project.text: Train a small GPT on text in your own language (Hindi, Tamil, Telugu…) or on your favourite author, on a free Colab GPU. Add temperature and top-k sampling and compare the outputs.

done_when: Your model generates text that looks like the training data
You can explain every line of your attention code

stages.title: RAG: answers from your own documents
stages.why: Models don't know your notes, PDFs or company data. RAG finds the right passages and hands them to the model, with citations.

resources.title: RAG From Scratch
resources.note: Short videos that build every RAG technique step by step.

resources.title: Advanced RAG on Hugging Face documentation
Sentence Transformers
resources.note: Free, local embedding models.

resources.title: pgvector
resources.note: Vector search inside PostgreSQL.

resources.title: Docling
resources.note: Turn PDFs into clean text and tables.

resources.title: Ragas
resources.note: Metrics for RAG quality.

project.title: A study assistant for your notes
project.text: Build a chat app over your own college notes and PDFs that cites the page for every answer and says “I don't know” when the notes don't cover it. (This is the Build Challenge project.)

done_when: Every answer shows where it came from
It refuses to guess when the answer isn't in your documents
You have 20 test questions with expected answers

stages.title: Agents and MCP
stages.why: Agents let a model take steps: call tools, read results and decide what's next. Learn to build ones that don't break.
topics: The agent loop: reason, act, observe

resources.title: Building effective agents
resources.note: Read this before any framework.

resources.title: Model Context Protocol
resources.note: The standard way to plug tools and data into AI apps.

project.title: An agent that asks before it acts
project.text: Build an agent that plans your study week from your notes and calendar through MCP, stops for your approval before changing anything, and has a hard limit on steps and cost.

done_when: Your agent stops and asks when it isn't sure
It can't loop forever or spend without limit
You can replay every step it took

stages.title: Evals, safety and security
stages.why: You can't improve what you don't measure, and every AI app can be attacked. Test before your users do.

resources.title: Promptfoo
resources.note: Automated tests and red-teaming.

resources.title: Arize Phoenix
resources.note: See every step your app took, locally.

project.title: Break your own app
project.text: Write 30 test cases for your RAG app and 10 attack prompts (for example, a PDF that says “ignore your instructions”). Run them on every change and fix what fails.

done_when: You run your evals with one command
You know your app's weakest spot and have a fix for it

stages.title: Fine-tuning and open models
stages.why: Sometimes prompting isn't enough. Learn when to fine-tune, and how to do it cheaply on a free GPU.
topics: When to fine-tune vs prompt vs RAG

resources.title: Unsloth documentation and free notebooks
resources.note: Fine-tune on a free Colab GPU.

resources.title: Ollama
resources.note: Run open models on your own laptop.

resources.title: DeepSeek-R1 paper
resources.note: How reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning.

project.title: Beat the prompt
project.text: Fine-tune a small open model (1–3B parameters) with QLoRA on a narrow task, such as turning messy notes into your college's exam format. Compare it with plain prompting, then run it locally with Ollama.

done_when: You can say when fine-tuning is worth it and when it isn't
Your fine-tuned model beats the base model on your test set

stages.title: Images, audio and multimodal
stages.why: Text is only one kind of generation. See how image, speech and vision-language models work, and where GANs and VAEs came from.

resources.title: Whisper
resources.note: Open speech-to-text you can run yourself.

resources.title: DCGAN tutorial
resources.note: Build a GAN once to see how generation started.

project.title: Lecture to notes
project.text: Build a demo that turns a recorded lecture into notes with Whisper, then generates a diagram for one key idea with a diffusion model. Host it on Hugging Face Spaces.

done_when: You can explain how diffusion turns noise into an image
Your demo works on a real recording

stages.title: Ship a real AI product
stages.why: Put it in front of real users: logins, limits, costs, speed and monitoring. This is what makes a project production-ready.

resources.title: AI Engineering
resources.note: The best single book on building AI products.

resources.title: Supabase
resources.note: Database, login and storage for your app.

resources.title: LMArena
resources.note: Compare models on real prompts.

resources.title: Artificial Analysis
resources.note: Speed and price of every model.

project.title: Launch it
project.text: Deploy your RAG or agent app for real users with login, rate limits, a cost dashboard and your evals running on every change. Get 10 people to use it and fix what they hit.

done_when: Real people use your app from a link
You know your cost per user and your slowest step
Your evals run before every deploy
